paras: The Fremont riot was a clash on the night of May 9, 1903, in Fremont, Ohio, in which Otto Mischke, a white man, was shot dead in a street fight with Black workers hired to replace strikers at the Clauss shear works, after which a crowd surrounded the jail demanding the three Black men arrested. Sheriff Mason held the crowd off, and Wheeler Kimbro, Lorenzo Martin and Walter Stratton were indicted for murder; Martin was convicted of manslaughter in 1904. White papers told it as a lynching averted, while the Cleveland Gazette defended the three as men who had fought off a strikers' mob.

According to the Cleveland Gazette, Black men from Cleveland and other northern Ohio towns had been hired to take the places of strikers at the Clauss works, and a Norwalk dispatch it reprinted said Kimbro had been shot at five times since arriving.

Late on May 9, guests leaving a party at the home of Albert Gummell (also printed Gommel) met a group of Black men in the street. The first wire said remarks were exchanged and the men "took offense" and fired first, but the New York Sun's dispatch said Ralph Gommell threw a stone that struck Kimbro on the head before the men drew revolvers. Mischke, 20, who lived at the Gummell house, was killed when he came out, and Albert Gummell was wounded; the first report also had his son R. C. Gummell shot in the leg.

A crowd that the Sun put at 200 and the Atlanta Constitution at "several hundred" then went to the jail and called on the sheriff to give up the prisoners. According to a Fremont report, from 1 to 4 a.m. Sheriff Mason stood on the steps of his residence and said he would shoot the first man who tried to break down the jail door. One version said the crowd made several attempts to get in; the Sun said it dispersed for want of a leader. Mayor Engler closed the saloons, and the prisoners were moved to Norwalk.

On May 12 Governor Nash refused the sheriff's request for troops to guard workers at the plant. Strikers stormed a Black family's house on the night of May 11, and about two dozen Black residents and their families left Fremont, mostly for Oberlin. Later a mob stoned the home of John Dixon, a Black worker who had not struck, and drove him from town.

On May 18 the grand jury indicted the three men and Richard and William Pettiford for murder, the Pettifords as accessories who had been "advisers." In Cleveland the Jewett Anti-Lynching League paid attorney Wm. T. Clark $30 to go to Fremont. In February 1904 a jury at Sandusky found Martin guilty of manslaughter, and he was sentenced to ten years and appealed; Kimbro and Stratton, facing a lesser shooting charge, were out on $1,000 bail by June. No report of the outcome of their cases or the Pettifords' appears in the coverage.

White papers first ran the wire under headlines such as "MOB READY WITH ROPE" and "NEGROES DID SHOOTING," calling the prisoners "Negro Murderers" and stating that the Black men began the shooting. Within a day the headlines turned to the sheriff, as in "WAS NO LYNCHING" in Savannah and "SHERIFF SAVES THREE NEGROES FROM MOB" in Washington.

The Cleveland Gazette answered on May 16 with "The Fremont Riot," saying "the truth" deserved a hearing and that the three had shot in self-defense after a mob of strikers and sympathizers assaulted them. It mocked the jail crowd as "two or three foolish admirers of the southern way of doing such things" and credited Ohio's anti-lynching law, under which three lynchings would have cost the county $15,000. The Gazette alone followed the case into 1904, printing a letter from the jail that called Mason "a man among men."

How the fight began is disputed: the first wire said the Black men fired first, the Sun that a white man threw a stone first, a Cleveland dispatch described a sidewalk scuffle, and the Gazette said the strikers attacked first. The prisoners said only that the published accounts were untrue and the "other side" more to blame.

reader.title: Fremont riot (1903)
bases: During a strike, a crowd of 200 or more surrounded the Fremont jail demanding three Black strikebreakers held for the killing of a white man, and the sheriff held it off (A6, A7, A8); the clash itself and the later expulsions of Black residents arose from the same strike (A14, A21, A26).

A crowd of 200 to several hundred tried to take three Black prisoners accused of murder from the jail (A6, A7, A8), but Sheriff Mason held it off and no one was killed by the mob (A7, A25); the one death was a white man shot in the street clash (A1, A6).

Independent dispatches from Fremont and Cleveland and the Cleveland Gazette agree on the shooting of Mischke, the arrest of the three men and the crowd at the jail held off by Sheriff Mason (A1, A6, A7, A9, A21), though they differ on who began the fight.

accounts.label: First Fremont wire
accounts.gist: Guests leaving the Gummell party exchanged remarks with Black non-union men, who took offense and started the shooting; William Kimbro was believed the killer and had partly confessed, 'it is said'.

accounts.label: Sun's Fremont dispatch
accounts.gist: Ralph Gommell made a remark, the men replied, and Gommell threw a stone striking Kimbro on the head before the men drew revolvers.

accounts.label: Cleveland dispatch
accounts.gist: Whites and Black men tried to push each other off the sidewalk, and in the scuffle the Black men drew revolvers and fired a volley.

accounts.label: Second Fremont wire
accounts.gist: The men were offended at Mrs. Albert Gommel's question as to who they were; Mischke was shot when he came to the door.

accounts.label: Cleveland Gazette
accounts.gist: A mob of strikers and sympathizers assaulted the three and injured at least one; they fired in self-defense.

accounts.label: Prisoners
accounts.gist: On their attorneys' advice they said only that the published accounts were untrue and the 'other side' was more to blame.

framing.detail: First-day headlines 'MOB READY WITH ROPE / Negro Murderers in Jail', 'NEGROES DID SHOOTING' and 'Negroes Start Trouble' stated that the Black men started the shooting.
Second-day reports centered the sheriff: 'WAS NO LYNCHING', 'SHERIFF SAVES THREE NEGROES FROM MOB', 'Three Negroes Nearly Lynched'.
A South Carolina digest noted that 'the Northern mob' wanted to lynch the three.

The Cleveland Gazette's 'THE FREMONT RIOT' set out 'the truth' against conflicting dailies, called the jail crowd 'cowards' and the shooting self-defense, and praised Sheriff Mason and Ohio's anti-lynching law.
The St. Paul Appeal set the expulsion of a Clauss worker among other wrongs to Black Americans.
